metadata.title: Writing Hookify Rules
metadata.purpose: Take apart the hookify-rule-vs-script case: explain why a markdown file Claude re-reads on every tool call catches a dangerous command without any code, then name the design trade — a straight regex only knows the exact characters you wrote down, so a slightly-too-broad pattern over-fires and a slightly-too-narrow one misses the identical danger. Lands the carry-out that a hookify rule is a markdown file Claude reads before every tool call, not a script — and it only catches exactly what its pattern says.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the hookify rule blocking rm -rf: fires reliably at the exact pattern, then either over-fires on a broad pattern or lets a rephrased danger through on a narrow one)

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. Someone wants a dangerous command caught before it runs, and reaches for code. But the block isn't a program — it's a rule in a file. So: what does one look like?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'How do I write a script to stop Claude from running rm -rf?', hesitates on 'script', corrects to 'rule', lands the real question

props.text:
How do I write a script
to stop Claude
from running rm -rf?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('script' -> 'rule') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: A hookify rule isn't code — it's a markdown file. It lives at dot-claude slash hookify dot name dot local dot md: a YAML frontmatter block on top, a plain message underneath. No build step, no restart. Claude re-reads the file before every single tool call — an edit takes effect on the very next one. Freshness over caching: nothing to compile, nothing to reload, nothing to remember.

shot.new_visual_element: A script/gears card receding while a markdown file card with a frontmatter divider grows in its place; the file path underneath; a 'read fresh, every call' tag

production_viz.label: A rule, not a script
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a card labelled 'custom hook script' with a terminal glyph, fading back. Right: a card labelled 'hookify rule' growing, showing a '---' frontmatter divider and two lines of YAML appearing beneath it. Below both, the file path '.claude/hookify.block-rm.local.md' fades in, then a small looping-arrows glyph with the words 'read fresh, every call'.

beats.narration_text: Five frontmatter fields carry the rule. Name, kebab-case, verb-first. Enabled, true or false. Event — bash, file, stop, prompt, or all — the moment the check runs. Pattern, a regex to match. And action, which defaults to warn — worth naming, because warn lets the operation through. Only block stops it outright. Watch the anchor: event bash, pattern matching rm -rf, action block. Claude reaches for the command, the regex matches, the tool call never fires.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — five field chips lighting in turn, then a rule card (event: bash / pattern: rm -rf / action: block), a command attempt arrowing into it, BLOCKED lighting in terracotta

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — five fields, then a block
production_viz.mechanic: Five small chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a field name (name / enabled / event / pattern / action), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A rule card appears centered: three stacked lines 'event: bash', 'pattern: rm -rf', 'action: block'. A command box reading 'rm -rf ~' arrows into the rule card; the rule card's text recolors to terracotta and a 'BLOCKED' chip lights beneath it. THIS EXACT SEQUENCE RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Get the pattern exact and the block fires every time — the check is a straight regex match, no judgment layered on top. That's the payoff, and it's also the ceiling. A regex only knows characters. Pattern the word log and you also catch catalog and login — blocking things nobody asked about. Pattern only rm -rf slash tmp and the identical danger typed against a different path sails straight through. Same match, opposite mistake. Determinism over meaning: you pay in the exact language of what you wrote down.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the same rule blocking three times in a row; then split: 'log' lighting up catalog/login as a false block, 'rm -rf /tmp' letting 'rm -rf ~' pass as a false miss

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — precision cuts both ways
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 RULE CARD RETURNS, identical, firing 'BLOCKED' three times in a row against three attempts. Then it splits into two cards side by side: left reads 'pattern: log' with 'catalog' and 'login' lighting up terracotta beneath it, labelled 'false block'; right reads 'pattern: rm -rf /tmp' with 'rm -rf ~' passing through unlit, labelled 'false miss'. A closing line beneath both: 'same match, opposite mistake'.

beats.narration_text: A hookify rule isn't a script you write — it's a markdown file Claude reads before every tool call, and it only catches exactly what its pattern says, no more, no less.

props.quote: A hookify rule isn't a script you write — it's a markdown file Claude reads before every tool call, and it only catches exactly what its pattern says, no more, no less.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I'm learning to write hookify rules for Claude Code — two rules to write, both as markdown files under dot-claude. First, a rule that blocks rm dash rf: event bash, pattern matching rm dash rf, action block. Call out why warn, the default, would silently let the command run, and what to do about rm dash rf slash tmp slipping past a too-narrow pattern. Second, a rule that flags edits to any dot-env file: event file, using a conditions block that checks file underscore path directly against a regex ending in dot env. Explain why matching only the new text being written would miss the edit itself. Third, read both files back and mark exactly where a slightly-too-broad pattern would over-fire, and where a slightly-too-narrow one would let the identical danger through. Go deeper: ask the same model what happens when two hookify rules with overlapping patterns fire on the same tool call — does one win, do both fire, and how would you know which rule actually caused the block if neither logged?

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm learning to write hookify rules for Claude Code. Two rules to write, both as markdown files under `.claude/`. (1) A rule that blocks `rm -rf`: event `bash`, `pattern` matching `rm -rf`, `action: block` — call out why `warn` (the default) would silently let the command run, and what to do about `rm -rf /tmp` slipping past a too-narrow pattern. (2) A rule that flags edits to any `.env` file: event `file`, using a `conditions` block that checks `file_path` directly against `\.env$` — explain why matching only the new text being written would miss the edit itself. (3) Then read both files back and mark exactly where a slightly-too-broad pattern would over-fire, and where a slightly-too-narrow one would let the identical danger through.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: ask the same model what happens when two hookify rules with overlapping patterns fire on the same tool call — does one win, do both fire, and how would you know which rule actually caused the block if neither logged?
